subject: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted vs current provider - follow-up
messages:
From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.inference>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.inference>, Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwood.inference>

Subject: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted vs current provider - recap and next steps

Hi Sam / Anna,

Thanks again for the call earlier — good discussion and appreciate you walking us through FinLytics' production traffic profile. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned: 

Summary of what you said FinLytics needs (please correct if I summarized incorrectly):
- End-to-end latency SLOs (inference request -> response delivered to client): p95 <= 250 ms, p99 <= 450 ms for single-turn text generation (typical payloads ~150 tokens).
- Peak concurrency target: sustained 180 concurrent requests, spiky bursts to ~300 concurrent requests for ~2-3 minutes.
- Throughput: average ~1,200 requests/min during peak window (payloads vary).
- Streaming requirements: streaming tokens to the client with first-token latency <= 120 ms and inter-token latency steady < 20 ms for streamed tokens.
- Availability/SLAs: prefer hosted option with ability to fallback to a lower-cost variant during capacity constraints; review of cold-start behavior is important.

What's Redwood proposing as the evaluation plan: 
1) Customer to share representative sample payloads and a 10-minute traffic trace (anonymized) — you've agreed to provide this by EOD Dec 2.
2) Redwood to run a targeted perf test against our hosted API using customer payloads and both streaming and non-streaming paths. We will test: p95/p99 end-to-end, first-token latency for streaming, concurrency at 100/180/300, and throughput to saturation.
3) Redwood solutions (Marissa) will provide an initial assessment of expected latency ranges (hosted) vs their reported numbers from current provider (NimbusAI) and propose tuning knobs (batching, kv caching, quant profiles).
4) Deliverables: perf test results (CSV + summary deck), proposed config for production (concurrency limits, autoscale settings), and a follow-up call to review results (target within 3 business days of receiving traces).

Attachments: I attached the FinLytics requirements sheet you shared (finlytics_perf_requirements.xlsx) and a short Redwood-hosted vs Nimbus SLA diff doc we referenced.

Next steps / asks from FinLytics: 1) share sample payloads + trace 2) confirm whether you want us to test on a streaming-enabled route only or both streaming + non-streaming.

I'll schedule a 30-minute review once we have results — propose Dec 6 or 7 afternoon PT.

Thanks,
Laura

Laura —

Thanks for the clear recap. Confirming the requirements below and responding to your asks:

- Confirmed SLOs: p95 <= 250 ms, p99 <= 450 ms (end-to-end) for single-turn generation (typical 120-180 tokens).
- Streaming: yes, we need both server-side streaming and client-level inter-token latency. First-token should be as low as possible; 120 ms is our target.
- Cold start: important — our current provider (NimbusAI) sees a noticeable degradation on cold starts for some models which pushes p99 above 600 ms; we'd like to understand Redwood's cold-start profile.
- Payloads/trace: attaching anonymized 10-minute trace and example payloads (in Drive link) — shared in the folder you listed.

We want Redwood to run both streaming + non-streaming perf tests. Also please include a run that exercises KV/prefix caching (we do have repeated prompt prefixes in 35% of requests).

Appreciate it — we can do the Dec 6 review after you run tests.

Best,
Sam

Subject: Re: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted vs current provider - technical notes

Hi Sam — thanks for the trace and details. A few technical notes / expectations from our side before we kick the perf runs: 

Initial expectations (hosted API):
- For typical single-turn generations (~150 tokens) on our hosted routes, end-to-end p95 in steady-state usually lands between ~90-220 ms and p99 between ~180-380 ms depending on model size and response length. With customer payloads we'll report concrete numbers.
- Streaming first-token: should be in the 50-140 ms range for most models; inter-token latencies are usually sub-25 ms once the stream is warmed. We'll measure cold-start impact separately.
- Concurrency behavior: our continuous-batching + worker pooling gives predictable latency up to configured concurrency — we expect to hit your 180 concurrent target with headroom, and we'll stress to 300 to validate. Autoscale/capacity smoothing can be tuned to avoid p99 spikes during bursts.
- Caching: since ~35% of your requests share prefixes, enabling prefix/KV caching can significantly reduce p95/p99 — we'll include cache-on vs cache-off test runs.

Tests we'll run (plan):
1) Baseline run using your payloads at 100/180/300 concurrent workers (non-streaming).
2) Streaming run: measure first-token latency and inter-token latency at 100/180/300 concurrency.
3) Cold-start run: bring new worker pool online and measure p95/p99 during the initial 5 minutes.
4) Cache vs no-cache runs.

Deliverables: raw CSV of per-request latencies, summary deck with p50/p95/p99 for each test condition, and recommended route config (batching thresholds, kv-cache TTL, quantization profile suggestion).

Immediate asks for FinLytics: please confirm the model(s) you plan to use in production (model name + typical generation length) and whether you have any hard constraints on tokenization (e.g., using byte-pair tokenization specifics). Also confirm whether streaming should be gRPC or HTTP chunked transfer for your client.

I'll kick off the perf cluster runs once we have the model names — we aim to have preliminary numbers within 48 hours of getting the model list and sample traces.

Thanks,
Marissa
